title: Choosing the Right Wood Species for Your Kitchen
excerpt: Oak, maple, walnut, cherry — each wood species brings different character to a kitchen. Here's how to choose wisely.
content:
# Choosing the Right Wood Species for Your Kitchen

Your choice of wood species is one of the most important design decisions you'll make for a custom kitchen. It affects not just aesthetics but durability, maintenance requirements, and how well your cabinetry ages.

## Hardwood Essentials

**White Oak** is currently our most popular choice. Its open grain takes stain beautifully, and its slight green-grey undertone pairs well with both warm and cool palettes. It's hard enough to resist kitchen dents and scratches, and it looks better at 20 years than at day one.

**Black Walnut** is the luxury choice — dark, rich, and impossible to imitate. Walnut is softer than oak, so we typically use it for doors and drawer fronts rather than boxes. The natural variation in colour, from chocolate brown heartwood to pale sapwood, makes every kitchen unique.

**Hard Maple** is the workhorse. Its tight, uniform grain gives a clean modern look, and it's the hardest of the common species. If you want a painted or light-stained kitchen, maple is usually the right call.

## The Grain Factor

Grain direction matters as much as species. Rift-sawn and quarter-sawn cuts are more dimensionally stable — they move less with seasonal humidity changes — and display a tighter, more linear grain pattern. They cost more, but for kitchen cabinetry that needs to stay aligned through years of steam and temperature swings, it's worth it.

## Making Your Choice

The best way to choose is to see full-size door samples in your actual space, in different lights. Book a consultation and we'll bring samples to you.

title: 5 Custom Cabinetry Trends Dominating 2024
excerpt: From fluted fronts to integrated pantry systems, here are the five design directions we're seeing most in custom kitchens this year.
content:
# 5 Custom Cabinetry Trends Dominating 2024

Custom kitchen design evolves quickly. Here's what we're building most of right now, and why these trends are worth paying attention to.

## 1. Fluted & Reeded Profiles

Vertical fluting on cabinet doors and island panels adds depth and handcraft character that flat-front doors can't match. It works in both traditional and contemporary settings. We're routing flutes directly into solid wood doors — no applied overlays.

## 2. The Invisible Pantry

Clients want to hide the pantry entirely. Floor-to-ceiling panelled doors that match the cabinet run, concealing a fully organised pantry behind them. The kitchen looks impossibly clean when the pantry is closed.

## 3. Limewash & Ceruse Finishes

Painted kitchens have matured past solid colour into textural territory. Cerused oak (where the grain is filled with contrasting lime putty) creates a tactile, artisanal feel that's unlike anything achievable with paint alone.

## 4. Mixed Material Islands

Painting the island a different colour or finishing it in a different wood from the perimeter cabinetry is now standard. We're seeing walnut islands in white oak kitchens, painted islands in all-wood kitchens, and steel-legged islands in traditional settings.

## 5. Integrated Appliance Columns

Refrigerators, dishwashers, and ovens fully integrated behind matching cabinet panels are increasingly the norm in higher-end projects. It requires precise planning but the result — a kitchen that looks like furniture — is worth the effort.

title: The Art of Hand-Cut Dovetail Joints
excerpt: Dovetails are the benchmark of fine woodworking. Here's why we still cut them by hand, and what makes the difference between a good dovetail and a great one.
content:
# The Art of Hand-Cut Dovetail Joints

A hand-cut dovetail is woodworking's signature. Its interlocking tails and pins create a joint with outstanding tensile strength that resists being pulled apart — which is exactly what you need for a drawer box or a cabinet carcase under decades of use.

## Why Still By Hand?

CNC routers can cut dovetails quickly and consistently. But a hand-cut dovetail has something a machine dovetail doesn't: the subtle variations in pin spacing and angle that declare it was made by a person. Those variations aren't imperfections — they're evidence of craft.

More practically, hand-cut dovetails can be adjusted. When fitting a drawer in a carcass that's ever so slightly out of square, a craftsman can pare half a millimetre from one pin and make the joint close perfectly. A machine-cut joint offers no such latitude.

## The Anatomy of a Good Dovetail

The ratio of the angle matters. We typically use a 1:8 ratio for hardwoods and 1:6 for softwoods. A too-steep angle weakens the joint; too shallow and you lose the mechanical advantage that makes the joint strong.

The fit should be hand-tight — firm but achievable without a mallet. Too loose and the joint will rattle; too tight and you risk splitting the wood when driving it home.

## What to Look For

When evaluating woodworking quality, look at the drawer corners. A gap you can slip a piece of paper into is fine. A gap you can see daylight through is not.

title: How to Properly Care for Hardwood Furniture
excerpt: Hardwood furniture gets better with age — if you treat it right. Here's our guide to oiling, cleaning, and protecting your investment.
content:
# How to Properly Care for Hardwood Furniture

The good news: hardwood furniture is far more resilient than most people think. The better news: proper care is straightforward.

## Oil Annually, Not More

For oil-finished furniture (which is most of what we make), one coat of Danish oil or hard wax oil per year is usually enough. Apply sparingly with a lint-free cloth, leave for 20 minutes, then buff away the excess. More oil isn't better — it builds up and turns sticky.

## Cleaning Day to Day

Wipe spills immediately with a barely damp cloth. Never use multi-surface sprays or furniture polish with silicone — they feel good in the short term but coat the wood pores and make future refinishing difficult.

For general cleaning, a cloth dampened with a small amount of Murphy's Oil Soap works well.

## Protecting From Heat and Light

UV light is wood's enemy over time. It bleaches walnut and cherry faster than you'd expect. If your furniture sits in direct sun, consider UV-filtering window film.

Heat and moisture cycles — a hot pan on a dining table, a glass of ice water sitting without a coaster — cause the surface finish to check and cloud. Use trivets and coasters, always.

## Scratches and Dents

Light scratches in oil-finished wood can often be buffed out with fine steel wool (0000 grade) and a wipe of oil. Deep dents in hardwood can sometimes be raised by putting a damp cloth over the dent and pressing with a hot iron — the steam causes the wood fibres to swell back.

For anything more serious, contact us.

title: Our 6-Step Process: From Consultation to Installation
excerpt: We've refined our process over 25 years to be thorough, transparent, and low-stress for clients. Here's exactly what happens from first contact to final handover.
content:
# Our 6-Step Process: From Consultation to Installation

We get asked often what working with us actually looks like. Here's our process, step by step.

## Step 1: Discovery Consultation (Week 1)

We meet at your space — always. We look at the room, take preliminary measurements, discuss your goals, your budget range, and your timeline. This is also where we listen to what you *don't* say: the things that bother you about the current space, what you're hoping to feel when you walk in.

## Step 2: Design & Proposal (Weeks 2–3)

Our designer produces a detailed proposal: drawings, material samples, finish options, and a fixed price. Nothing is approximate — you know what you're getting before you sign anything.

## Step 3: Deposit & Scheduling

A 40% deposit confirms your project and locks your slot in the build schedule. We're typically 6–10 weeks out from deposit to build start.

## Step 4: Build

Your project is built in our Portland workshop. You're welcome to visit. We send progress photos at key milestones.

## Step 5: Finishing & Quality Check

Every piece is finished and inspected before it leaves the workshop. Doors are hung, drawers fitted, hardware installed. We test everything.

## Step 6: Installation & Handover

Our installation team handles delivery and fitting. We don't leave until everything is right. Final payment is due on completion.

title: Why Sustainable Wood Sourcing Matters to Us
excerpt: We've sourced only FSC-certified or locally salvaged timber since 2015. Here's why that decision matters, and what it means for the wood in your project.
content:
# Why Sustainable Wood Sourcing Matters to Us

In 2015, we made a commitment: every piece of timber we use would be either FSC-certified, locally salvaged, or sourced from small-scale regional mills with verified sustainable practices. Here's why, and what it means for your project.

## The Problem with Conventional Timber Supply Chains

Much of the hardwood sold in the US passes through supply chains with no verified source-of-origin documentation. Old-growth timber and illegally logged wood can enter the market looking identical to sustainably harvested wood. We chose to require documentation because we believe the burden of proof should be on the supplier, not the customer.

## What FSC Certification Actually Means

FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) certification tracks timber from forest to finished product. Certified forests maintain biodiversity, protect waterways, and commit to replanting. It's not a perfect system, but it's currently the most rigorous widely available.

## Our Regional Preference

Wherever possible, we source from Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia mills. Shorter supply chains mean lower transport emissions, better traceability, and — often — better quality. We've built relationships with several small mills who let us select logs directly.

## Salvaged Timber

For some projects, salvaged timber is the right choice: old barn wood, reclaimed Douglas fir from demolition projects, urban trees felled by the City of Portland. Each piece has a history. It's denser, often more figured, and already dry.

## What This Means for You

For most species, sustainable sourcing adds 5–15% to material costs. We absorb some of this and disclose the rest. We think it's worth it.
